Behind these APIs is a software layer connecting and optimizing communications networks around the world. With the Twilio APIs, you can build applications that help your users send messages, make phone calls, look up phone numbers, and more. In Twilio's ecosystem, each product corresponds to an API. For example, Twilio Messaging corresponds to the Messaging API. Although each API has its own unique features, they all share a common set of principles and practices. This consistency lets you work with different Twilio APIs in a similar way. You can use the APIs directly over HTTPS or through Twilio SDKs available for several programming languages. This section covers how to work with the Twilio APIs: Make requests to the Twilio APIs , including authenticating your requests, choosing the right content type, and handling webhooks. Work with Twilio API responses , including specifying response formats, paginating results, and handling errors. Handle mutations and conflicts . Follow API best practices . Need some help? We all do sometimes; code is hard. Get help now from our support team , or lean on the wisdom of the crowd by browsing the Twilio tag on Stack Overflow. With API keys, you control which users and applications have access to your Twilio Account's API resources, and you can revoke access at your discretion. If your Twilio application uses one of the client-side SDKs, then you need to use API keys to create Access Tokens . (information) Info Twilio API credentials are a Region-specific resource. If your Account uses Twilio Regions , refer to Manage Regional API Credentials . When using the Twilio CLI to create regional profiles, you must specify both --region and --edge flags together. See Regional CLI usage for details. Why you should use API keys API keys are a powerful and flexible way to manage access to Twilio resources. Create individual API keys for specific purposes and individuals. You have complete control of the lifecycle of the API credentials for your Twilio Account. For example, you can issue separate API keys to different developers or subsystems within your application. If a key is compromised or no longer used, revoke it to prevent unauthorized access. You can further reduce security risks by using Restricted API keys to provide minimum and specific levels of access. Types of API keys (information) Best practices for working with API keys For guidance on securing your API credentials and configuring your environment: Learn how to safely store your API keys in environment variables in the How to Set Environment Variables blog post . Learn more about general API security best practices in the Guide to Basic API Security Best Practices blog post . The API key types are Main , Standard , and Restricted (Key resource v1 only). The following table describes each type: Key type Access permissions Create in Console Create with REST API Main Full access to all Twilio API resources. Equivalent to using your Account SID and Auth Token for API requests. Yes No Standard Access to all Twilio API resources, except for Accounts ( /Accounts ) or Keys ( /Accounts/{SID}/Keys , /v1/Keys ) resources. Yes Yes Restricted Customized, fine-grained access to specific Twilio API resources. Learn more about Restricted API keys . Yes Yes ( v1 only ) What's next? API keys represent the required credentials that you'll use to authenticate to Twilio's REST API and to create and revoke Access Tokens . (information) Info If your API key requires access to the Accounts ( /Accounts ) or Keys ( /Accounts/{SID}/Keys , /v1/Keys ) endpoints, then you'll need to use a Main key. You can create Main keys only in the Twilio Console . Types of keys The API key types are Main , Standard , and Restricted (Key resource v1 only). The following table describes each type: Key type Access permissions Create in Console Create with REST API Main Full access to all Twilio API resources. Equivalent to using your Account SID and Auth Token for API requests. Yes No Standard Access to all Twilio API resources, except for Accounts ( /Accounts ) or Keys ( /Accounts/{SID}/Keys , /v1/Keys ) resources. Yes Yes Restricted Customized, fine-grained access to specific Twilio API resources. Learn more about Restricted API keys . Yes Yes ( v1 only ) Key Properties Property name Type Required PII Description Child properties sid SID<SK> Optional Not PII The unique string that we created to identify the Key resource. Pattern: ^SK[0-9a-fA-F]{32}$ Min length: 34 Max length: 34 friendlyName string Optional Not PII The string that you assigned to describe the resource. dateCreated string<date-time-rfc-2822> Optional Not PII The date and time in GMT that the resource was created specified in RFC 2822 format. dateUpdated string<date-time-rfc-2822> Optional Not PII The date and time in GMT that the resource was last updated specified in RFC 2822 format. flags array[string] Optional Not PII Create an API key POST https://iam.twilio.com/v1/Keys (warning) Warning To create Standard API keys with the API, you must use one of the following credentials: your Account SID and Auth Token, a Main API key, or a Restricted API key with the permission for /twilio/iam/api-keys/create . (information) Best practices for working with API keys For guidance on securing your API credentials and configuring your environment: Learn how to safely store your API keys in environment variables in the How to Set Environment Variables blog post . Learn more about general API security best practices in the Guide to Basic API Security Best Practices blog post . Request body parameters Encoding type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded Schema Example Property name Type Required PII Description Child properties accountSid SID<AC> required Not PII The SID of the Account that created the Payments resource. Pattern: ^AC[0-9a-fA-F]{32}$ Min length: 34 Max length: 34 friendlyName string Optional PII MTL: 30 days A descriptive string that you create to describe the resource. It can be up to 64 characters long. keyType string Optional Not PII The `KeyType` form parameter is used to specify the type of key you want to create. Default Behavior : If `KeyType` is not specified, the API will generate a standard key. Restricted Key : If `KeyType` is set to `restricted`, the API will create a new restricted key. In this case, a policy object is required to define the permissions. policy Optional Not PII The `Policy` object is a collection that specifies the allowed Twilio permissions for the restricted key. For more information on the permissions available with restricted API keys, refer to the Twilio documentation . Select from available examples createStandardKey createRestrictedKey Copy code block { "FriendlyName" : "foo" , "AccountSid" : "ACaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa" } Create a Standard API key Node.js Python C# Java Go PHP Ruby twilio-cli curl Report code block Copy code block 1 // Download the helper library from https://www.twilio.com/docs/node/install 2 const twilio = require ( "twilio" ); // Or, for ESM: import twilio from "twilio"; 3 4 // Find your Account SID at twilio.com/console 5 // Provision API Keys at twilio.com/console/runtime/api-keys 6 // and set the environment variables. See http://twil.io/secure 7 // For local testing, you can use your Account SID and Auth token 8 const accountSid = process.env. TWILIO_ACCOUNT_SID ; 9 const apiKey = process.env. TWILIO_API_KEY ; 10 const apiSecret = process.env. TWILIO_API_SECRET ; 11 const client = twilio (apiKey, apiSecret, { accountSid: accountSid }); 12 13 async function createNewKey () { 14 const newApiKey = await client.iam.v1.newApiKey. create ({ 15 accountSid: "ACXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX" , 16 friendlyName: "Mario's API key" , 17 }); 18 19 console. log (newApiKey.sid); 20 } 21 22 createNewKey (); Response Copy response 1 { 2 "sid" : "SKaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa" , 3 "friendly_name" : "Mario's API key" , 4 "date_created" : "Mon, 13 Jun 2016 22:50:08 +0000" , 5 "date_updated" : "Mon, 13 Jun 2016 22:50:08 +0000" , 6 "secret" : "foobar" , 7 "policy" : null 8 } The response contains a sid property and a secret property. Store the secret in a secure location, because you won't be able to retrieve it again. Twilio uses the Key resource's sid and the secret as the credentials when making API requests. See http://twil.io/secure 7 // For local testing, you can use your Account SID and Auth token 8 const accountSid = process.env. TWILIO_ACCOUNT_SID ; 9 const apiKey = process.env. TWILIO_API_KEY ; 10 const apiSecret = process.env. TWILIO_API_SECRET ; 11 const client = twilio (apiKey, apiSecret, { accountSid: accountSid }); 12 13 async function createNewKey () { 14 const newApiKey = await client.iam.v1.newApiKey. create ({ 15 accountSid: "ACXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX" , 16 friendlyName: "Mario's API key" , 17 keyType: "restricted" , 18 policy: { 19 allow: [ "/twilio/messaging/messages/read" ], 20 }, 21 }); 22 23 console. log (newApiKey.sid); 24 } 25 26 createNewKey (); Response Copy response 1 { 2 "sid" : "SKaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa" , 3 "friendly_name" : "Mario's API key" , 4 "date_created" : "Mon, 13 Jun 2016 22:50:08 +0000" , 5 "date_updated" : "Mon, 13 Jun 2016 22:50:08 +0000" , 6 "secret" : "foobar" , 7 "policy" : { 8 "allow" : [ 9 "/twilio/messaging/messages/read" 10 ] 11 } 12 } Fetch a Key resource GET https://iam.twilio.com/v1/Keys/{Sid} Returns a representation of the API key. (warning) Warning For security reasons, Twilio returns the secret field only when the API key is first created and never includes the secret field when you fetch the resource. Your application should store the API key's SID and secret in a secure location to authenticate to the API. To verify that you granted the requester permission to your account resources, Twilio requires authentication on every API request. When you create a Twilio account, Twilio generates an Account SID and an Auth Token. The Auth Token provides broad account access and should be protected like a high-privilege password. Supported authentication methods Twilio supports three authentication methods. Choose based on your security requirements and integration needs: OAuth 2.0 — Recommended for new integrations Short-lived access tokens, as brief as one minute Scoped to specific permissions Best for third-party apps and delegated access Requires token refresh mechanism API Keys — Recommended for server-side apps Main API Key: Provides broad account access (avoid for new integrations) Standard API Key: Full account access with SID isolation Restricted API Key: Scoped to specific capabilities (recommended for new integrations) Auth Token authentication — Legacy option Provides broad account access Should only be used when OAuth 2.0 or API keys are not supported Treat as last-resort option Choosing the right authentication method Whenever the integration supports OAuth 2.0 or a Restricted API Key, use it. These options allow you to scope access to the capabilities your integration needs. This limits the potential impact of a leaked credential. Auth Tokens and Main API Keys provide broad account access. Although they remain supported, treat them as legacy or last-resort options rather than the default for new integrations. The following table compares key attributes of each authentication method: Method Scope control Token lifetime Recommended use Security level OAuth 2.0 Highly scoped Short-lived (configurable) Third-party apps, delegated access Highest Restricted API Key Scoped to capabilities Long-lived (until revoked) Server-side apps High Standard API Key Account-level access Long-lived (until revoked) Admin access, account management Medium Auth Token Broad account access Long-lived (until rotated) Legacy integrations only Low OAuth 2.0 and SDK support OAuth 2.0 provides the strongest security posture for API authentication. To simplify implementation, Twilio provides SDK support for OAuth . These SDKs refresh tokens and reduce the amount of code that you must implement for authentication. This reduces the risk of expired token errors. Best practices for all authentication methods Implement the following practices regardless of which authentication method you choose: Prefer short-lived OAuth 2.0 access tokens where appropriate. Rotate client credentials and signing keys according to organizational policy. Revoke credentials immediately when you suspect compromise. Grant each integration only the permissions it needs. Keep authentication logic on the server side and out of browser-delivered code. Never hardcode credentials in source code or client-side apps. Store all credentials in a secrets manager . Visit the Developer Hub On this page Practices to avoid Keep credentials out of code or repositories Secure credentials storage Don't reuse or overshare credentials Don't substitute authentication with network controls Keep authentication mechanisms current Why these mistakes happen Common consequences of anti-patterns Next steps Copy as markdown Copy and view Copy as markdown View as markdown Open in assistant Open in ChatGPT Open in Claude Open in Cursor Open in Perplexity Build with AI Connect your AI agent Install Twilio Skills Authentication anti-patterns Poor authentication practices lead to credential compromise. Even with strong authentication mechanisms available, mistakes in how you store, transmit, or manage credentials undermine all security protections. The following patterns cover common practices that significantly increase risk. These patterns appear frequently in compromised integrations. Avoid these patterns. Practices to avoid Poor authentication practices make credential compromise easy for attackers and incidents expensive to remediate. The following practices increase risk: Keep credentials out of code or repositories Never embed Auth Tokens, Main API Keys, or Restricted API Keys in browser code or mobile apps. Never hardcode credentials in source files including temporary commits you plan to remove. Never hardcode credentials in infrastructure templates, configuration files, or Docker images. Never commit credentials to version control repositories or CI/CD systems. Secure credentials storage Never store credentials in plain-text files on disk. Never store credentials in unencrypted local storage like browsers or mobile devices. Never log full authorization headers, request bodies containing secrets, or environment variables. Never transmit credentials through email, chat systems, screenshots, or issue trackers. Don't reuse or overshare credentials Never share credentials with people, vendors, or support channels. Grant controlled access. Never reuse one credential across multiple unrelated apps or environments. Never reuse credentials after team member changes, vendor relationships end, or deployments change. Never grant access to production credentials to all users. Implement role-based access control. Don't substitute authentication with network controls Never treat a private network connection (VPN, private subnet, firewalls) as a replacement for authentication. Never assume internal only means you don't need to protect credentials. Never substitute network security for app security. Keep authentication mechanisms current Never ignore security advisories for Twilio SDKs, dependencies, frameworks, or infrastructure. Never delay applying security patches to systems that can access Twilio APIs. Never use deprecated or end-of-life versions of authentication libraries. Why these mistakes happen Anti-patterns simplify initial development through the following poor practices: Embedding credentials speeds prototyping. Hardcoding involves less work than integrating a secrets manager. Sharing credentials avoids waiting for access approvals. Skipping secrets management feels like progress until an incident occurs. The development time saved gets lost in incident response, emergency credential rotation, and security audits. Common consequences of anti-patterns These mistakes lead to the following consequences: Credentials exposure in GitHub , Docker registries , or AWS Simple Storage Service (S3) buckets Automated attackers discovering exposed credentials within minutes Unauthorized API usage, SMS pumping, or identity theft Incidents affecting your customer data and trust Regulatory fines and compliance violations Emergency incident response and credential rotation Audit failures and remediation work Next steps Implement secure credential practices: Secrets management — storing and protecting credentials securely Secure authentication — choosing the right authentication method Defense-in-depth strategy — comprehensive security layers Incident response — responding to exposed credentials GitHub secret scanning documentation Need some help? Visit the Developer Hub On this page Choose needed webhooks Respond to webhooks Mock webhook requests for development Create automated tests for webhooks Run your app on a public URL Configure your public URL with Twilio Validate that webhook requests come from Twilio Test your webhooks with live traffic Promote your web app to staging and production Get answers Copy as markdown Copy and view Copy as markdown View as markdown Open in assistant Open in ChatGPT Open in Claude Open in Cursor Open in Perplexity Build with AI Connect your AI agent Install Twilio Skills Get Started with Twilio Webhooks This guide walks you through receiving Twilio webhooks in your web app, from finding the right webhooks to running in production. This quickstart guide doesn't apply to a specific Twilio product, language, or platform. Choose needed webhooks Your app can use webhooks with the following Twilio products: Voice Messaging Conversations (classic) Authy Proxy Video Status Facebook Messenger Twilio can also provide information over webhooks: Debugging Usage Alert Your app doesn't require all webhooks. Respond to webhooks With your chosen webhooks, map out how you want to respond to each. Some Twilio webhooks require a response in Twilio Markup Language (TwiML) or JSON. The TwiML you send back to the webhook varies based on what product you are using: TwiML for Programmable Voice TwiML for Programmable Messaging TwiML for Programmable Fax Informational Twilio webhooks require a standard HTTP 200 OK response. This shows that your web app received the webhook. Mock webhook requests for development Once you have identified the webhooks you are planning to use, it's time to write some code! For ad-hoc testing purposes during development, you may find it worthwhile to set up mock HTTP requests to your app. We suggest either using a command-line tool like curl , or a desktop app like Postman . Use the sample webhook requests found in the Twilio documentation as starters for your own requests, or send Twilio webhooks to a service like RequestBin to capture the HTTP request being sent. Create automated tests for webhooks After doing some initial validation of your code, you can write automated tests using your preferred testing framework. Once you deploy your app, you can check the Twilio Debugger for errors when a webhook is sent to your app. Those HTTP requests would make excellent candidates for additional tests for your web app framework. For test-driven development (TDD), you may consider swapping the order of this step and the previous step. Run your app on a public URL Twilio needs to send webhook requests to an internet-reachable URL. Choose from two methods: Deploy your web app code to a development or test server on the public internet. Expose a local environment to the internet using an HTTP tunneling tool like ngrok . (warning) Company network security might not allow tunnels Your network security team might block ngrok or other HTTP tunnels. In those cases, configure a development or testing server that Twilio can reach before deploying your webhook project to a production environment. To learn how to use ngrok to develop webhooks locally, see Webhook testing . Configure your public URL with Twilio Configure your webhook target URL for Twilio requests in the Twilio ecosystem. Twilio Voice might need a webhook URL for inbound voice calls, inbound messages, or inbound faxes. Twilio messaging might need a webhook URL for outbound messages. The typical API request parameter for the webhook URL gets named callback or statusCallback . To send an outbound message, the TwiML <Message> verb provides an attribute to set the status webhook URL. Validate that webhook requests come from Twilio Once Twilio can send requests to your web app, start validating that Twilio sends your incoming webhooks. To learn more, see Webhooks Security specifically the validating Twilio requests section. If your integration tests use your validation process, Update your integration tests, update the tests. Many test frameworks can set environment variables for test mode as well as production. Keep account credentials outside of your code as a best practice. Test your webhooks with live traffic To test live traffic depends on which webhooks you use, but you can start making phone calls to your Twilio number, sending text messages, or whatever else you have built. Try to exercise as many corner or edge cases as possible with your app. This checks any assumptions you left out of your unit or integration tests. Promote your web app to staging and production Promote your web app to a staging environment, then to production. At each step, update the webhook URL you use with Twilio for the correct environment. Test your webhook with SSL enabled and the certificates you use in production. Twilio webhooks don't work on HTTPS endpoints with self-signed SSL certificates. To learn more, see Webhooks Security . Before passing production traffic through your web app, decide how Twilio should authenticate and sign the webhooks it sends you. The Webhooks configuration API sets the authentication at the URL level. Get answers If you have any concerns, see Webhooks FAQ . Need some help? We all do sometimes; code is hard. Copy as markdown Copy and view Copy as markdown View as markdown Open in assistant Open in ChatGPT Open in Claude Open in Cursor Open in Perplexity Build with AI Connect your AI agent Install Twilio Skills Authenticate webhooks with OAuth 2.0, Basic, or Digest Your webhook endpoint can require Twilio to authenticate itself as any other API client would. Twilio supports OAuth 2.0 client credentials, HTTP Basic, and HTTP Digest. (warning) Set the default rule to use anything but HTTP Basic authentication A default Rule matches every otherwise-unmatched webhook URL. This results in sending Basic credentials to every destination that Twilio calls. Twilio rejects that with error 59202 . Scope Basic authentication to an exact-match or prefix-match Rule , or use OAuth 2.0 or HTTP Digest on the default Rule. Authentication and signing solve different problems and work independently. Authentication proves Twilio can call your endpoint. A signature proves the integrity of the request body in transit. Use authentication, signatures, or both, over secure HTTP. Use inline credentials or an AuthProfile Twilio stores credentials in a required Webhook Setting auth object in one of two forms. Form When to use it Inline ( source: INLINE ) Each Setting has its own credentials. Recommended for most accounts. AuthProfile ( source: REFERENCE ) Several Settings share one set of credentials, so you rotate them in one place. The standalone AuthProfile resource stores one set of credentials. To use it, create the AuthProfile, then set a Setting's auth to "source": "REFERENCE" with the AuthProfile's id as the authProfileId . OAuth 2.0 To fetch an access token from your authorization server, Twilio uses the client credentials flow . Twilio then sends the token as a Bearer token in the Authorization header of each webhook. When a token nears expiry, Twilio requests a replacement. Prerequisites An OAuth 2.0 authorization server with client credentials support, and from it: The token endpoint URL A client ID A client secret Optionally, a scope Optionally, an audience Request body parameters Field Necessity Description scheme or type required OAUTH2 . Use scheme for inline credentials, type for an AuthProfile. tokenUrl required Your authorization server's token endpoint. clientId required The OAuth 2.0 client identifier. clientSecret required The OAuth 2.0 client secret. Write-only, and never returned in a response. scope optional The scope Twilio requests. audience optional The audience Twilio requests. clientCredentialsAuthMethod optional CLIENT_SECRET_POST (default) or CLIENT_SECRET_BASIC . Create an OAuth 2.0 AuthProfile Make a POST request to the AuthProfiles resource. Copy code block 1 curl -X POST https://webhooks.twilio.com/v1/Webhooks/AuthProfiles \ 2 -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ 3 -u {API_KEY_SID}:{API_KEY_SECRET} \ 4 -d '{ 5 "type": "OAUTH2", 6 "friendlyName": "Example authorization server", 7 "tokenUrl": "https://auth.example.com/oauth2/token", 8 "clientId": "{CLIENT_ID}", 9 "clientSecret": "{CLIENT_SECRET}", 10 "scope": "webhooks:write", 11 "clientCredentialsAuthMethod": "CLIENT_SECRET_POST" 12 }' Returns 201 Created . Save the returned id . Reference it from a Setting's auth object, then apply that Setting with a Webhook Rule . What Twilio sends to your authorization server With CLIENT_SECRET_POST , Twilio puts the credentials in the form body. Copy code block 1 curl -X POST https://auth.example.com/oauth2/token \ 2 -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" \ 3 -d "grant_type=client_credentials" \ 4 -d "client_id={CLIENT_ID}" \ 5 -d "client_secret={CLIENT_SECRET}" If you set a scope or an audience, Twilio includes them. Copy code block 1 curl -X POST https://auth.example.com/oauth2/token \ 2 -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" \ 3 -d "grant_type=client_credentials" \ 4 -d "client_id={CLIENT_ID}" \ 5 -d "client_secret={CLIENT_SECRET}" \ 6 -d "scope=webhooks:write" \ 7 -d "audience=https://api.example.com" With CLIENT_SECRET_BASIC , Twilio sends the client ID and secret in an Authorization: Basic header instead of the body. What your authorization server must return A JSON body containing at least access_token , token_type , and expires_in . The token type must be Bearer , and expires_in must be at least 300 seconds. Copy code block 1 { 2 "access_token" : "eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9..." , 3 "token_type" : "Bearer" , 4 "expires_in" : 3600 5 } When token retrieval fails If Twilio can't exchange your credentials for a token, it retries twice, 250 milliseconds apart. If those also fail, Twilio drops the webhook and logs error 97001 in the Twilio Debugger . Twilio tries again after 300 seconds, and webhooks matching that Setting may be dropped during that window. Common causes are an unreachable authorization server, rotated or removed credentials, and a token issued with a type other than Bearer . HTTP Basic Request body parameters Field Necessity Description scheme or type required BASIC . username required The username Twilio sends. password required The password. Write-only, never returned. Copy code block 1 curl -X POST https://webhooks.twilio.com/v1/Webhooks/AuthProfiles \ 2 -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ 3 -u {API_KEY_SID}:{API_KEY_SECRET} \ 4 -d '{ 5 "type": "BASIC", 6 "friendlyName": "Partner endpoint", 7 "username": "{USERNAME}", 8 "password": "{PASSWORD}" 9 }' HTTP Digest To use HTTP Digest, include the same username and password fields as Basic but set "type": "DIGEST" . Copy code block 1 curl -X POST https://webhooks.twilio.com/v1/Webhooks/AuthProfiles \ 2 -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ 3 -u {API_KEY_SID}:{API_KEY_SECRET} \ 4 -d '{ 5 "type": "DIGEST", 6 "friendlyName": "Legacy endpoint", 7 "username": "{USERNAME}", 8 "password": "{PASSWORD}" 9 }' No authentication Every setting requires the auth parameter. When Twilio shouldn't authenticate itself, set the scheme to NONE . Copy code block { "auth" : { "source" : "INLINE" , "value" : { "scheme" : "NONE" } } } Manage AuthProfiles List all AuthProfiles Secrets are never included. Copy code block 1 curl -X GET https://webhooks.twilio.com/v1/Webhooks/AuthProfiles \ 2 -u {API_KEY_SID}:{API_KEY_SECRET} Fetch one AuthProfile Copy code block 1 curl -X GET https://webhooks.twilio.com/v1/Webhooks/AuthProfiles/{AUTH_PROFILE_ID} \ 2 -u {API_KEY_SID}:{API_KEY_SECRET} Update an AuthProfile Only friendlyName is editable. Copy code block 1 curl -X PATCH https://webhooks.twilio.com/v1/Webhooks/AuthProfiles/{AUTH_PROFILE_ID} \ 2 -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ 3 -u {API_KEY_SID}:{API_KEY_SECRET} \ 4 -d '{ "friendlyName": "Example authorization server (EU)" }' To change tokenUrl , clientId , clientSecret , or any other credential field, create a different AuthProfile and point your Settings to the created AuthProfile . Delete one AuthProfile To delete one AuthProfile, make a DELETE request of the AuthProfiles resource with its ID. Copy code block 1 curl -X DELETE https://webhooks.twilio.com/v1/Webhooks/AuthProfiles/{AUTH_PROFILE_ID} \ 2 -u {API_KEY_SID}:{API_KEY_SECRET} A successful request returns 204 No Content . A failed request returns 409 Conflict as a Setting still references it. To resolve the error, find the dependent Settings, then change where they point or delete them. Copy code block 1 curl -X GET 'https://webhooks.twilio.com/v1/Webhooks/Settings?authProfileId={AUTH_PROFILE_ID}' \ 2 -u {API_KEY_SID}:{API_KEY_SECRET} Rotate credentials with no downtime You can't change anything in an AuthProfile except its friendlyName . To rotate credentials, replace the resource. Create an AuthProfile with the updated credentials. Create a Setting that references the AuthProfile. Test the added Setting against your endpoint. Shift your Rule onto the added Setting. If you want to validate on live traffic first, make the shift gradually. Delete the old Setting. Delete the old AuthProfile. What's next?
